did_you_know.text: Did you know? Psalm 77 opens with a musical heading: “For the director of music; according to Jeduthun,” and is attributed to Asaph. The heading indicates that the psalm was intended for musical performance or direction.
Did you know? In verse 2, the word “voice” is repeated twice. This repetition emphasizes the intensity of the cry and the psalmist’s plea for God to listen to him.
Did you know? The psalmist describes distress that is not limited to the daytime: even at night, his hand is stretched out in prayer, yet his soul still finds no comfort.
Did you know? In verse 5, the distress is expressed through both body and speech: the psalmist describes eyes that will not close, inner turmoil, and an inability to speak.
Did you know? Alongside the memory of “my song in the night,” the psalmist carries on an inner dialogue and searches for answers within his spirit; thus, the night becomes a time of self-examination.

Did you know? Verses 8–10 contain a series of rhetorical questions about rejection, the end of steadfast love, the forgetting of mercy, and the withholding of compassion. These questions express the depth of the psalmist’s crisis.

Did you know? In verse 11, the direction of the psalmist’s thoughts changes: after his difficult questions, he turns his attention to the years of the “right hand of the Most High” and to God’s work throughout the generations.

Did you know? The psalmist chooses to confront his distress through remembrance: he recalls the deeds of the Lord and the wonders performed in the past, rather than remaining focused only on his questions.
Did you know? In verse 17, the waters are described as though they see God, are terrified, and tremble. This is a poetic description that gives nature a response of awe.
Did you know? The psalm contrasts God’s way through the sea, where no visible footprints remain, with his clear guidance of his people: he leads them “like a flock” by the hand of Moses and Aaron.
